messages.content: A user swears her password is right, but login fails every time. She signed up as Priya.Nair@Example.com. Our login handler lowercases the email before looking it up, but signup stored it exactly as typed. Is that enough to lock her out?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
stored_key=Priya.Nair@Example.com
buggy_login=False
fixed_login=True

Yes - that mismatch alone locks her out. Signup stored the key `Priya.Nair@Example.com`, but login looks up the lowercased form, so the lookup misses and the correct password compares against nothing: buggy_login=False. The password was never wrong; the identity key was.

The fix is to normalize at BOTH ends, with one shared function: signup stores the trimmed, lowercased address, and login normalizes the same way before lookup - fixed_login=True. Normalizing only at login strands every mixed-case account created earlier, so a real fix also migrates existing keys (lowercase them in place) rather than just patching the code. Email local parts are technically case-sensitive, but every major provider treats them as case-insensitive, so normalizing is the pragmatic, industry-standard choice.

Our signup form trims whitespace from every field, including the password. A user who deliberately set a password with a leading space can never log in, because the login form does not trim. I reproduced it in miniature - what is the actual defect and the right fix?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
stored=leading-space-9
login_exact_typed=False
login_without_space=True

The defect is asymmetric normalization: signup silently rewrote the credential (`pw.strip()`), so the secret stored is `leading-space-9`, a different password from the one the user chose. Login compares exactly, so login_exact_typed=False - the user's true password is rejected - while the stripped variant they never picked succeeds: login_without_space=True.

The right fix is to never silently trim passwords at all. Whitespace can be a legitimate part of a passphrase, and a password field is not a name field. Trim display fields (name, email) if you must; treat the password as opaque bytes from both forms. If a legacy signup already trimmed some passwords, those accounts' real passwords ARE the trimmed ones now - flag them for reset rather than guessing.

We migrated password storage from a legacy fast hash to a modern KDF last month. Since then, every account created before the migration gets 'invalid password' even with the right password. New accounts work fine. Here is the shape of our verify path - what went wrong?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_old_account=False
buggy_new_account=True
migrating_old_account=True
upgraded_prefix=s256

The verify path only speaks the new format. A pre-migration row stores an `md5$...` digest, but verify_buggy hashes the attempt with the new function and compares - two different algorithms will never produce equal strings, so buggy_old_account=False while buggy_new_account=True. The users' passwords never changed; the verifier forgot how to read old rows. (Both hashes here are toy stand-ins at demo parameters - the shape of the bug is what matters.)

The standard repair is dual-verify with opportunistic upgrade: branch on the stored prefix, verify legacy rows with the legacy function, and on success immediately re-hash with the modern KDF and overwrite - migrating_old_account=True, and the row now carries the upgraded_prefix=s256 marker. Accounts migrate themselves as their owners log in; whatever remains in the legacy format after a deadline gets force-reset.

A reviewer flagged our digest comparison for using == instead of a constant-time compare. Our tests pass either way, so what does the flag actually protect against, and how do I show the team the two are interchangeable in verdict but not in behavior?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
attempt_verdicts: eq=True compare_digest=True
attempt_verdicts: eq=False compare_digest=False
attempt_verdicts: eq=False compare_digest=False

The verdicts are identical - every attempt above prints the same result under == and under compare_digest, which is why your tests cannot tell them apart. The difference is in HOW the comparison fails. == on strings short-circuits: it returns at the first differing character, so the response time leaks how many leading characters were right. Against a digest that leak is mostly theoretical (an attacker would need to guess a hash prefix, not a password), but against directly-compared tokens - reset codes, API keys, MACs - it is a real oracle.

hmac.compare_digest compares every byte regardless of where the mismatch is. The rule to adopt: any comparison of a secret or a digest of a secret uses compare_digest (or the framework equivalent), everywhere, as a habit - not because each call site is exploitable, but because the one that is will not announce itself. Note this demo shows verdict equivalence only; it does not and cannot measure the timing difference.
Security review says our login leaks which accounts exist. The messages are 'No account for that email' and 'Incorrect password'. Does the wording really matter if both are just errors?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_unknown=No account for that email
buggy_known_wrong_pw=Incorrect password
fixed_unknown=Invalid email or password
fixed_known_wrong_pw=Invalid email or password

It matters because the two messages form an oracle. buggy_unknown returns 'No account for that email' while buggy_known_wrong_pw returns 'Incorrect password' - an attacker feeds a list of emails, keeps the ones that produce the second message, and now owns a verified account list for phishing or credential stuffing, without ever guessing a password.

The fix collapses both failures into one response: fixed_unknown and fixed_known_wrong_pw both return 'Invalid email or password'. Same for the other channels reviewers check next: identical HTTP status, near-identical response time (run a dummy hash verification for unknown accounts so the timing matches too), and the same generic message on the password-reset form. Your own UX loses nothing - a real user who mistypes learns only that something was wrong, which is all they need.
Following up on enumeration: our API returns 404 when the email is unknown and 401 when the password is wrong, even though the message text is now generic. Is the status code alone still a leak?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_unknown_status=404
buggy_known_status=401
fixed_unknown_status=401
fixed_known_status=401

Yes - the status code is the same oracle wearing a different coat. The body text is now identical, but buggy_unknown_status=404 versus buggy_known_status=401 still sorts any email list into 'exists' and 'does not exist' for anyone who can read a response code, which is every script ever written.

Return one status for every credential failure: fixed_unknown_status=401 and fixed_known_status=401. While you are in there, sweep the sibling channels for the same leak in other encodings: response-time differences (hash-check a dummy value for unknown accounts), account-recovery flows that confirm existence, and registration forms that say 'this email is already taken' before any verification - that last one is sometimes accepted as a UX trade-off, but it should be a decision, not an accident.

Our users table has both 'Admin@shop.com' and 'admin@shop.com' as separate accounts, created months apart, with different passwords and order histories. Signup checks for duplicates with an exact match. How did we end up with twins, and what closes the hole?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
first=created
second=created
accounts_now=2
fixed_first=created
fixed_second=duplicate rejected
fixed_accounts_now=1

Exact-match duplicate checks treat case variants as different identities, so the second signup sailed through: accounts_now=2 distinct rows for what every mail system considers one mailbox. The twins then diverge - different passwords, histories, and support nightmares - and the security version is worse: a lookalike account squatting on a case variant of a staff address.

Close it by making the normalized form the identity: check and store by strip()+lower() (plus whatever provider rules you adopt), as signup_fixed shows - fixed_second=duplicate rejected, fixed_accounts_now=1. Enforce it in the database with a unique index on the normalized column, not just in application code, because the next import script will not read your signup handler. Then merge the existing twins deliberately, with a human deciding which history survives.

Two of our users picked the same password, and an intern noticed their stored hashes are identical. Our demo store hashes with a bare SHA-256 and no salt. Why is identical output a problem, and what does salting change in the printout?

arguments.code:
import hashlib
def bare(pw):
    return hashlib.sha256(pw.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
def salted(pw, salt):
    return hashlib.sha256((salt + ":" + pw).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
print("bare_alice=" + bare("sunshine-1"))
print("bare_bob=" + bare("sunshine-1"))
print("same=" + str(bare("sunshine-1") == bare("sunshine-1")))
print("salted_alice=" + salted("sunshine-1", "salt-alice"))
print("salted_bob=" + salted("sunshine-1", "salt-bob"))
print("salted_same=" + str(salted("sunshine-1", "salt-alice") == salted("sunshine-1", "salt-bob")))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
bare_alice=9404c25d424fddc5
bare_bob=9404c25d424fddc5
same=True
salted_alice=f4e420487a142a91
salted_bob=293d1771aacbcf8f
salted_same=False

With a bare fast hash, the password IS the only input, so identical passwords produce identical digests - same=True. Anyone who obtains the table learns which users share passwords without cracking anything, and precomputed rainbow tables turn the most common passwords into plaintext at lookup speed. One crack also opens every twin account at once.

A per-user random salt makes the inputs differ, so salted_same=False even for the same password: each row must be attacked individually, and precomputation is useless. Two honest caveats: this demo uses SHA-256 purely to show the shape - production storage needs a slow, memory-hard KDF (Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt) with the salt it generates internally; and a salt is not a secret - it is stored beside the hash. Its job is uniqueness, not concealment.

We want a lockout after repeated failed logins, but a previous attempt locked out our CEO during a board demo because an attacker kept failing AS her. Our toy policy counts failures per account. What policy does the miniature implement instead, and why?

arguments.code:
from collections import defaultdict
attempts = defaultdict(int)
def login(ip, email, ok):
    key = (ip, email)
    if attempts[key] >= 5:
        return "throttled: this source must wait"
    if ok:
        attempts[key] = 0
        return "welcome"
    attempts[key] += 1
    return "invalid"
for i in range(5):
    login("203.0.113.9", "ceo@example.com", False)
print("attacker_source=" + login("203.0.113.9", "ceo@example.com", False))
print("ceo_from_office=" + login("198.51.100.4", "ceo@example.com", True))
print("ceo_counter_from_office=" + str(attempts[("198.51.100.4", "ceo@example.com")]))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
attacker_source=throttled: this source must wait
ceo_from_office=welcome
ceo_counter_from_office=0

The miniature throttles per (source, account) pair instead of per account. The attacker's five failures exhaust only their own pair - attacker_source gets 'throttled: this source must wait' - while the CEO signing in from the office is a different pair with a clean counter: ceo_from_office=welcome. A pure per-account lockout hands anyone on the internet a denial-of-service button for any named account, which is exactly what your demo incident was.

Layered practice: progressive delays or CAPTCHA per (IP, account), a separate slower counter per account that triggers step-up verification rather than a hard lock, alerting on distributed failures against one account (many IPs, one target - the pattern this scheme alone misses), and a success resetting only its own pair's counter, as shown by ceo_counter_from_office=0. Hard lockouts belong to admin-assisted recovery, not to an automatic counter a stranger can ring.

A user registered with the email '  Marta@Example.COM  ' - pasted with spaces - and now mail to her bounces and she cannot log in with the clean address. Signup stored the raw string. Where should cleanup have happened?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_login_clean=False
stored_key=marta@example.com
fixed_login_clean=True

At the boundary, once, before storage. The buggy signup stored the raw paste - spaces and all - as the account key, so the mailbox of record literally contains spaces (hence the bounces) and no clean login can ever match it: buggy_login_clean=False.

Normalize identifiers on the way IN - strip surrounding whitespace, lowercase - store only the canonical form, and have login apply the identical normalization: fixed_login_clean=True. Note the deliberate contrast with passwords: identifiers get normalized because they are public labels with one canonical form; passwords are secrets and must be stored and compared exactly as chosen. Teams that apply one rule to both fields produce either un-loginable users (this bug) or silently weakened passwords (the trimming bug).

Our session store records created_at but nothing ever checks an expiry. A security audit sampled live sessions and found some created months ago still authenticating. I mocked the store with a fixed 'now' - what does the audit see, and what was missing?

arguments.code:
NOW = 1_800_000_000
sessions = {"s-old": {"user": "amy", "created": NOW - 90*86400},
            "s-mid": {"user": "ben", "created": NOW - 40*86400},
            "s-new": {"user": "cy", "created": NOW - 3600}}
def valid_buggy(sid):
    return sid in sessions
ancient = [sid for sid, s in sessions.items() if NOW - s["created"] > 30*86400]
print("live_sessions=" + str(len(sessions)))
print("older_than_30d=" + str(len(ancient)))
print("oldest_still_valid=" + str(valid_buggy("s-old")))
TTL = 12*3600
def valid_fixed(sid):
    s = sessions.get(sid)
    return bool(s) and NOW - s["created"] <= TTL
print("fixed_oldest_valid=" + str(valid_fixed("s-old")))
print("fixed_new_valid=" + str(valid_fixed("s-new")))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
live_sessions=3
older_than_30d=2
oldest_still_valid=True
fixed_oldest_valid=False
fixed_new_valid=True

The audit sees a store where validity means existence. With no TTL anywhere, live_sessions=3 includes older_than_30d=2 sessions, and the 90-day-old token still authenticates: oldest_still_valid=True. A session id leaked in March is a working credential in June; the store has become a permanent second password database, one entry per login ever.

What was missing is an expiry decision: an absolute lifetime (and usually an idle timeout) stored with the record and checked on every use - valid_fixed rejects the ancient session (False) while keeping the fresh one (True). Also add the unglamorous half: a sweeper that deletes expired rows, because a check without cleanup leaves the table growing forever and the audit trail full of corpses.
Users report that after clicking Logout they can paste their old session cookie into a fresh browser and they're straight back in. Our logout clears the cookie and redirects. What did we forget?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
after_buggy_logout=dana
after_fixed_logout=None

You forgot the server. Logout cleared the cookie - a client-side gesture - but the session record still sits in the store, so the pasted cookie authenticates: after_buggy_logout=dana. Clearing a cookie tells YOUR browser to forget the key; it does nothing to the lock. Anyone holding a copy of that id - from a log, a shared machine, a screenshot - keeps the access the user believes they ended.

Logout must delete or invalidate the server-side record, then clear the cookie as tidiness: after_fixed_logout=None. Same principle at every 'revoke' surface: password change, admin disable, 'sign out everywhere' - all of them are server-side deletions. The cookie is a pointer, never the thing itself.

Our app issues a session id on the landing page before login, and keeps the same id after the user authenticates. A tester set his session id to a value he chose, then logged in, and the chosen id still worked. Walk me through the flaw.

arguments.code:
sessions = {}
def visit(sid):
    sessions.setdefault(sid, {"user": None})
    return sid
def login_buggy(sid, user):
    sessions[sid]["user"] = user
    return sid
def authenticate(sid):
    s = sessions.get(sid)
    return s["user"] if s else None
import itertools
counter = itertools.count(1)
def login_fixed(sid, user):
    sessions.pop(sid, None)
    new = "srv-%04d" % next(counter)
    sessions[new] = {"user": user}
    return new
visit("attacker-chosen")
login_buggy("attacker-chosen", "victim")
print("fixated_id_authenticates_as=" + str(authenticate("attacker-chosen")))
new = login_fixed("attacker-chosen", "victim")
print("after_rotation_old_id=" + str(authenticate("attacker-chosen")))
print("new_id_authenticates_as=" + str(authenticate(new)))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
fixated_id_authenticates_as=victim
after_rotation_old_id=None
new_id_authenticates_as=victim

That is session fixation. The application accepted a session id supplied from outside (visit created a record for the tester's chosen value), then upgraded that very id to an authenticated session at login - so an attacker who can plant an id in a victim's browser (a link, a subdomain cookie, a shared kiosk) knows a working authenticated credential in advance: fixated_id_authenticates_as=victim.

The fix is rotation at the privilege boundary: the moment authentication succeeds, destroy the pre-login session and issue a fresh, server-generated id - after_rotation_old_id=None, new_id_authenticates_as=victim. Apply the same rotation at every privilege change (password change, MFA step-up, role elevation): a session's id should never survive becoming more powerful than it was when issued.

Complaint of the week: 'I log in on my laptop and my phone session dies.' Our store keeps one session per user and a new login overwrites it. Users think it's a bug; honestly it was a line of code from v1. What are the real options?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
single_policy_phone_survives=False
multi_policy_devices=laptop,phone

Neither behavior is a bug - an undocumented policy is the bug. The single-session store makes the second login silently evict the first: single_policy_phone_survives=False, which users experience as random logouts. The multi-session store keeps both: multi_policy_devices=laptop,phone.

Pick deliberately and write it down. Single-session suits high-sensitivity apps (banking) IF the displaced device gets a clear 'signed out because you signed in elsewhere' message instead of silent death. Multi-session suits almost everything else, paired with a 'your devices' page listing live sessions with revoke buttons - that list is also your audit surface for the logout and revocation fixes. What you cannot ship is the accidental middle: eviction as a side effect of a dict keyed by user, discovered by your users before your team.

We changed a compromised user's password and confirmed the main sessions were killed - but the account kept making API calls for a week afterward. The trail led to a 'remember me' token issued months earlier. Why did it survive?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
before_change_valid=True
after_change_buggy=True
after_change_fixed=False

Because the remember-me token was its own credential universe. Nothing in its validation path ever asked whether the password had changed since it was minted. Password change killed the session store; the remember-me store was a separate dict with a separate lifetime, so after_change_buggy=True and the token calmly re-established full sessions for a week.

Version the long-lived tokens by credential state: stamp each remember-me token with the account's password version at issue, and reject it when the versions diverge - after_change_fixed=False. The same version stamp protects password-reset tokens and API keys if you want changes to propagate. The general law: enumerate EVERY artifact that can authenticate as the user - sessions, remember-me cookies, refresh tokens, API keys, app passwords - and give credential change a kill path to each one.

Our sessions have a 30-minute idle timeout, yet a penetration test kept a session alive for 11 days by pinging it every 20 minutes. The client is furious; engineering says the timeout 'works as coded'. Who is right?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
age_days=11
idle_only_valid=True
with_absolute_cap_valid=False

Both - and that is the problem. The idle timeout works exactly as coded: the session was never idle for 30 minutes, so idle_only_valid=True at age_days=11. A sliding window alone cannot bound total lifetime; a patient script (or a stolen cookie on a cron job) renews it forever.

Sessions need two clocks. The idle timeout bounds inactivity; an absolute cap bounds total age from creation no matter how active - with_absolute_cap_valid=False under an 8-hour cap. When the absolute cap hits mid-work, the graceful pattern is step-up re-authentication (confirm password or MFA) that mints a genuinely new session, not a quiet extension of the old one's created timestamp - otherwise the cap is decorative. Choose caps by sensitivity: hours for admin and banking surfaces, days for low-risk consumer apps, but never infinity-by-renewal.

After we ship a release, half the support tickets say 'I keep getting logged out every few clicks' - but only until they close the tab. Our two app servers each keep sessions in local memory. Reproduce the mechanism.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
request_to_a=gus
request_to_b=None
shared_store_b=gus

The mechanism is split-brain session storage. Login landed on server A and wrote the session into A's memory: request_to_a=gus. The load balancer sent the next click to B, whose memory has never heard of sid-1: request_to_b=None - a logout. The next click may hit A again and 'log back in', which is why the symptom flickers per click and vanishes per tab.

Sessions are shared state and must live in a shared store (Redis, the database) or the balancer must pin users to one server (sticky sessions - workable, but it makes deploys and failovers hurt). The shared store gives shared_store_b=gus from any node. Diagnostic tell for the field: logouts that correlate with nothing the user did, begin right after a scale-out or deploy, and affect a fraction of users at a time - check where sessions live before you check the sessions themselves.

Boundary bug hunt: our session check is `if now > expires_at: reject`. A session with a 15-minute token was accepted at the exact moment it should have died, and an auditor flagged the one-second window. Is this pedantry or a real defect?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
t=1899 buggy=True fixed=True
t=1900 buggy=True fixed=False
t=1901 buggy=False fixed=False

A real defect, of the small honest kind. With `now > expires` as the rejection test, the instant t=1900 itself passes: at the boundary the buggy check still says valid while the fixed check (accept only while now < expires) does not. The printed sweep shows the two disagreeing at exactly one second - expires - and agreeing everywhere else.

One second of extra session life harms nobody directly. The auditor's point is what the boundary reveals: expiry semantics were never specified, so three implementations in the codebase will make three choices (this one, >=, and one comparing against created+ttl recomputed with a different ttl). Specify it once - 'a token is valid strictly before its expiry instant' is the common convention, matching JWT's exp claim - implement it in one shared function, and pin it with a boundary test at expires-1, expires, expires+1 so the next refactor cannot quietly move the line.

A user tapped 'sign out' on her phone and was horrified to find her office desktop signed out too - she wanted the desktop to stay. Our sessions table has one row per user holding a single token. What design change does she actually need?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
desktop_after_phone_logout=tok-shared
desktop_after_fixed_logout=tok-d
phone_after_fixed_logout=None

One row per user means one identity per human, shared by every device - so any device's logout deletes the only token and every device dies: desktop_after_phone_logout=tok-shared. The user's mental model is per-device sessions; the schema's model is per-user. The schema wins every fight it picks with a user.

Model sessions per (user, device): one row per login, with device label, created, last seen. Logout deletes its own row - desktop_after_fixed_logout=tok-d while phone_after_fixed_logout=None. This one schema change also buys you the 'your devices' management page, per-device revocation when a phone is lost, and the concurrent-session policy from the neighboring complaint - which is why session modeling is worth doing once, properly, instead of patching symptoms.

Our 'keep me signed in' checkbox is decorative: the code sets a 30-day session cookie whether or not the box is ticked. A user on a shared family computer discovered this. Show the defect and the honest behavior.

arguments.code:
def cookie_lifetime_buggy(keep_signed_in):
    return 30*86400
def cookie_lifetime_fixed(keep_signed_in):
    return 30*86400 if keep_signed_in else 0
print("buggy_unchecked_days=" + str(cookie_lifetime_buggy(False)//86400))
print("fixed_unchecked=" + str(cookie_lifetime_fixed(False)))
print("fixed_checked_days=" + str(cookie_lifetime_fixed(True)//86400))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_unchecked_days=30
fixed_unchecked=0
fixed_checked_days=30

The defect is a preference read by the UI and ignored by the issuer: buggy_unchecked_days=30 regardless of the box, so a user who explicitly declined persistence on a shared machine stayed signed in for a month for the next family member to find.

Honest behavior: unchecked means a session cookie (lifetime 0 = dies with the browser) - fixed_unchecked=0; checked means the persistent 30-day cookie - fixed_checked_days=30 - backed by a server-side record with the same lifetime so the two cannot drift. The checkbox is a consent surface, not decoration: whatever it promises is what the cookie must do. Audit the rest of the form with the same suspicion - a 'remember this device' for MFA that ignores its box is the same bug wearing a security costume.

Our API verifies the signature on its HMAC tokens but a pen-tester replayed a token that expired three days ago and got straight in. The token format is header.payload.signature built in the test below. What check is missing?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
signature_ok=True
expired_by_days=3
buggy_accepts=True
fixed_accepts=False

The expiry check. The signature proves the token is genuinely yours and untampered - signature_ok=True - but a signature says nothing about WHEN the token may be used. verify_buggy never opens the payload, so a token expired_by_days=3 sails through: buggy_accepts=True. A signature without a lifetime turns every issued token into a permanent credential, and tokens leak into logs, screenshots, and browser history far more easily than passwords.

Verify claims after the signature: exp (reject at or after it), and as the next records show, iss, aud, nbf, and token type. fixed_accepts=False with the same signature check plus `now < exp`. Note the demo token is a toy HMAC construction for illustration - the defect class is identical in real JWT libraries when claims validation is switched off or never enabled.

Our billing service accepts access tokens minted for the profile service. Both use the same signing key, and the tokens carry aud and iss claims that nobody checks. Is sharing a key across services itself the bug?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_billing_accepts_profile_token=True
fixed_billing_accepts_profile_token=False
fixed_profile_accepts=True

Sharing a key is a risk factor; skipping claim checks is the bug. The token honestly declares aud=profile - it was minted for one audience - but accept_buggy ignores claims entirely, so buggy_billing_accepts_profile_token=True. Any token from any service on the shared key becomes a skeleton key for all of them, and the blast radius of one low-value service's token leak is the whole platform.

Check iss and aud on every request: accept_fixed binds the token to its audience - fixed_billing_accepts_profile_token=False, fixed_profile_accepts=True. Defense in depth then reduces the sharing risk itself: per-service keys or asymmetric signing (services hold only public keys) so a compromised verifier cannot mint. But even with perfect key hygiene, an unchecked aud claim is a door left open by design.

Every morning around daylight-saving changes - and randomly for users whose laptops have drifting clocks - we get a burst of 'token expired' rejections for tokens issued minutes earlier. Our verifier allows zero clock skew. What is the standard allowance and how does it change the verdicts?

arguments.code:
def verify(exp, now, leeway):
    return now < exp + leeway
exp = 1_800_000_000
skewed_now = exp + 45
print("skew_seconds=45")
print("zero_leeway=" + str(verify(exp, skewed_now, 0)))
print("leeway_120=" + str(verify(exp, skewed_now, 120)))
print("leeway_120_rejects_600_late=" + str(verify(exp, exp + 600, 120)))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
skew_seconds=45
zero_leeway=False
leeway_120=True
leeway_120_rejects_600_late=False

No two clocks agree perfectly, and a verifier with zero tolerance treats ordinary drift as expiry. Here the client's clock runs skew_seconds=45 ahead, so a token at its true expiry boundary is rejected: zero_leeway=False. Around DST transitions and on machines with sick NTP, that produces exactly your burst pattern - clustered, time-correlated, and infuriating because the tokens are 'obviously' fresh.

The standard allowance is a small leeway - 60 to 120 seconds is typical - applied symmetrically to exp, nbf, and iat: leeway_120=True for the drifted client, while a genuinely dead token is still refused: leeway_120_rejects_600_late=False. Leeway is not a longer lifetime; it is an admission that 'now' is an estimate. Keep it small, keep it explicit in config, and log the observed skew when you reject - a fleet-wide skew spike is an infrastructure alarm, not a user error.

Our refresh tokens rotate on every use, which sounded airtight - until a review showed the OLD refresh token still works after rotation if you replay it fast. The store just overwrites. What does a correct rotation do with a replayed predecessor?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_replay_old=True
fixed_first_use=rotated to rt-3
fixed_replay_old=REUSE DETECTED - family revoked
fixed_after_reuse_current=family revoked

A rotated-out refresh token should be dead, and its reappearance should be treated as theft evidence. refresh_buggy accepts both generations - buggy_replay_old=True - so an attacker holding a stolen old token and the legitimate client can refresh in parallel forever, each rotation invisible to the other.

Correct rotation keeps the family ledger: the current token rotates once (fixed_first_use=rotated to rt-3), predecessors are remembered as used, and presenting a used token triggers the alarm - fixed_replay_old=REUSE DETECTED - family revoked - revoking the ENTIRE family, which is why fixed_after_reuse_current=family revoked too. The legitimate user re-authenticates once; the attacker loses everything. The design principle: reuse of a rotated credential is never a race condition to tolerate, it is the detection signal the rotation exists to produce.

A user pasted a support screenshot showing our app URL with ?access_token= right in it, and the same URLs are all over our access logs and our analytics vendor's dashboard. The API also accepts tokens in a header. What is the exposure and the migration?

log_line = "GET /api/orders?access_token=tok-live-123 200"
def token_in(line):
    part = line.split("access_token=")[1]
    return part.split(" ")[0]
print("leaked_token=" + token_in(log_line))
print("copies_in_log_systems=3")
def accept_buggy(query_tok, header_tok):
    return query_tok or header_tok
def accept_fixed(query_tok, header_tok):
    return header_tok
print("buggy_query_accepted=" + str(accept_buggy("tok-live-123", None)))
print("fixed_query_accepted=" + str(accept_fixed("tok-live-123", None)))
print("fixed_header_accepted=" + str(accept_fixed(None, "tok-live-123")))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
leaked_token=tok-live-123
copies_in_log_systems=3
buggy_query_accepted=tok-live-123
fixed_query_accepted=None
fixed_header_accepted=tok-live-123

A token in a URL is a token in every system that touches URLs: the access log (leaked_token=tok-live-123, lifted straight out of one line), analytics, error trackers, browser history, and the Referer header sent to any third-party resource the page loads - copies_in_log_systems=3 before you count screenshots. Migrate to the Authorization header (or a secure cookie for browser flows): accept_fixed ignores the query parameter entirely - fixed_query_accepted=None - while the header path works unchanged: fixed_header_accepted=tok-live-123. Do it in two steps if clients lag: first log-and-warn on query tokens so you can find the offenders, then reject. And treat already-leaked tokens as compromised: anything that ever appeared in a log line gets revoked, not just deprecated.

Our mobile app stores an opaque token - just a random string the server looks up. A new dev 'optimized' the profile endpoint to parse it as a JWT because it contains dots, and to skip the server lookup when parsing succeeds. What breaks?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
token_revoked_on_server=True
buggy_auth=kim
fixed_auth=None

Revocation breaks. The token was revoked server-side (token_revoked_on_server=True), but the string happens to contain two dots, so parse_as_jwt 'succeeds' on its shape and the buggy path never consults the store: buggy_auth=kim - a dead credential resurrected by a parser. Shape is not type: dots in an opaque string are punctuation, not claims, and anything 'parsed' out of it is fiction the client supplied.

Opaque tokens have exactly one source of truth - the server's lookup (introspection): auth_fixed returns fixed_auth=None because the store says revoked. The two token families are different tools: self-contained tokens (JWT) trade revocation for statelessness; opaque tokens trade a lookup for instant revocability. The bug class to hunt in review is any code path that lets a token choose which family it belongs to - that choice belongs to the issuer, recorded at issue time, never inferred from the string.

Our token library is configured to accept any algorithm the token header names. In our toy model the verifier holds an RSA public key as a string, and a token whose header says HS256 gets verified using that same string as an HMAC secret. Explain the failure in one paragraph a junior can follow, at the mechanism level.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
forged_sig=010d376a017f91da
buggy_accepts_forged=True
fixed_accepts_forged=False

The failure is algorithm confusion, and the junior version is: the token gets to choose the lock it is checked against. The server publishes its RSA public key - by design, everyone can know it. If the verifier obeys a header that says 'actually, treat this as an HMAC token', it uses that PUBLIC string as the HMAC secret, and since the secret is public, anyone can mint a valid signature at home: buggy_accepts_forged=True, with the forged signature computed in the open above. (Toy keys and truncated signatures - the logic flaw is the lesson, not the crypto.)

The defense is pinning: the verifier, not the token, decides the algorithm - one expected alg per key, configured server-side, everything else rejected before signature work begins: fixed_accepts_forged=False. Modern libraries do this when you pass an explicit algorithms allowlist; the vulnerability lives in the integrations that pass 'any'.

A read-only integration token was used to DELETE records through our API. The token is genuine, unexpired, and scoped 'read'. The delete handler checks authentication and nothing else. Where exactly is the missing line?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy=deleted invoice-9
fixed=forbidden: scope

Between 'who are you' and 'do it'. delete_buggy asks only whether a token exists - authentication - and never what the token is FOR - authorization by scope. So a read-scoped credential deletes: buggy=deleted invoice-9. Scopes are not documentation; they are half the token's contract, and an endpoint that ignores them silently promotes every low-privilege integration to full access.

The missing line is the scope check inside every handler (or a middleware table mapping routes to required scopes): fixed=forbidden: scope. While fixing, audit the route table for the same shape - handlers written before scopes existed often check 'any valid token'. And scope generously-named tokens down: a 'read' token that is widely distributed to partners should be assumed public for design purposes, which is exactly why it must never write.

Design said access tokens live 15 minutes. An auditor decoded one of ours and found exp 30 days after iat. Nobody remembers changing it; the config default in our framework is '30d' and the line overriding it was never written. How do you catch this class of drift?

issued = 1_800_000_000
config = {"access_token_ttl": "30d"}
def ttl_seconds(v):
    n = int(v[:-1]); u = v[-1]
    return n * {"m": 60, "h": 3600, "d": 86400}[u]
actual = ttl_seconds(config["access_token_ttl"])
print("actual_ttl_days=" + str(actual//86400))
print("design_ttl_minutes=15")
print("drift_factor=" + str(actual//900))
def audit(cfg):
    return "FAIL" if ttl_seconds(cfg["access_token_ttl"]) > 3600 else "ok"
print("audit=" + audit(config))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
actual_ttl_days=30
design_ttl_minutes=15
drift_factor=2880
audit=FAIL

You catch it by testing the artifact, not the intention. The decoded token is the ground truth: actual_ttl_days=30 against design_ttl_minutes=15 - a drift_factor=2880 times longer than designed, inherited silently from a framework default nobody chose. Long-lived access tokens defeat revocation strategy: with no per-request store lookup, a stolen one is a month-long key.

The durable fix is an audit that decodes real issued tokens (or reads the effective config) and asserts the security invariants: audit=FAIL here because TTL exceeds the one-hour ceiling the test enforces. Put the same assertions on the other silent defaults: cookie flags, leeway, algorithm allowlists, session TTLs. Framework defaults are optimized for demos that work, not for your threat model - every security-relevant default your system inherits should appear in a test that would fail if it changed.

A stolen refresh token was replayed from a different device and network and our API happily minted fresh access tokens. The refresh token record stores only the token and the user. What binding was missing?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_other_device=True
fixed_other_device=False
fixed_same_device=True

The binding between the token and the client it was issued to. refresh_buggy compares only the string, so possession is identity - buggy_other_device=True - and a refresh token, being long-lived and powerful, is the single worst credential to leave unbound. It is the master key that mints all the others.

Bind refresh tokens at issue to something the thief does not have: the client identity (confidential clients authenticate themselves at the refresh call), and where the platform supports it, a device key - the token is usable only with a signature from a private key held in the device's keystore (DPoP / mTLS token binding in the real protocols). The toy version compares stored device and client: fixed_other_device=False, fixed_same_device=True. Binding does not make theft impossible; it makes the stolen string insufficient, which is the whole game with bearer credentials.

Classic report from a customer: 'I changed the number at the end of the invoice URL and saw someone else's invoice.' Our handler fetches the invoice by id and returns it to any signed-in user. Reproduce and repair in miniature.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_mia_reads_noahs=True
fixed_mia_reads_noahs=False
fixed_noah_reads_own=True

That is an IDOR - insecure direct object reference. The handler authenticated the user and then never authorized the object: buggy_mia_reads_noahs=True. Sequential ids make it a browsing feature; even unguessable ids only slow it down, because ids leak in emails, exports, and shared links.

The repair is to scope every fetch by the caller: `WHERE id = ? AND owner = ?`, so another user's object is indistinguishable from a missing one - fixed_mia_reads_noahs=False, fixed_noah_reads_own=True. Return 404, not 403, for out-of-scope objects so the endpoint does not confirm existence. Then sweep for the pattern systematically: any handler whose query contains an id from the request but no owner/tenant predicate is a finding, whether or not anyone has exploited it yet.

Our frontend hides the Admin button unless the user object says is_admin, and the API trusts an is_admin field sent in the request body 'because only the frontend sets it'. A curl command later... explain what the API got wrong.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_forged_flag=admin action performed
fixed_forged_flag=forbidden

The API confused presentation with authorization. Hiding a button is a UX choice; the server then treated a client-supplied field as a fact about the user, and clients can supply anything - buggy_forged_flag=admin action performed with a hand-written request, no frontend involved. Anything the client sends is a claim, not evidence.

Authorization facts live server-side, derived from the authenticated identity: the fixed handler looks the user up in the server's own store and ignores the body's flag - fixed_forged_flag=forbidden. The review rule that catches the whole family: grep the authorization code for any decision that reads role, admin, owner, or tenant from request input (body, query, headers the client controls). Those values may select WHAT the user is asking for; they may never testify about WHO the user is.

We revoked a contractor's 'export' permission at 09:00. At 09:40 she exported again successfully. Permissions are cached in the session service with a one-hour TTL and no version check. Was the cache 'working'?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
revoked_at=09:00 attempt_at=09:40
buggy_can_export=True
fixed_can_export=False

The cache was working exactly as caches do - serving a stale truth inside its TTL: buggy_can_export=True, forty minutes after revocation. The defect is architectural: a revocation is a security event, and a design where security events take up to an hour to matter has quietly redefined 'revoke' as 'revoke eventually'.

Two standard repairs, often combined. Version-stamp the permission set: every grant change bumps a version, cached entries carry theirs, and a mismatch forces a refresh before the check - fixed_can_export=False immediately. Or keep TTLs but add explicit invalidation on the write path (grant/revoke publishes a cache purge). What you cannot do is promise instant revocation in the UI while the enforcement layer runs on eventual consistency. Match the mechanism to the promise: display the TTL honestly, or invalidate eagerly.

A user was removed from the 'finance' group on Monday, but her access token - minted Friday with the groups baked in as claims - still opens finance reports on Wednesday. The reports service never re-checks membership. Whose lifetime is wrong?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_day3_finance=True
fixed_day3_finance=False
fixed_day3_staff=True

The claim's lifetime is wrong. Baking group membership into a 7-day token freezes Monday's org chart into a credential that Wednesday still honors: buggy_day3_finance=True. The token is not lying about Friday; the service is treating a Friday fact as a Wednesday fact.

The tension is real - self-contained claims are fast, live lookups are fresh. The standard settlements: keep token lifetimes short (minutes) so staleness is bounded and refresh re-reads membership; or check sensitive groups against the live directory regardless of claims; or version the claims like the permission cache. fixed_day3_finance=False with the live check, while legitimate access survives: fixed_day3_staff=True. Decide per resource: a wiki tolerates claim staleness, payroll does not. The failure is applying one freshness policy - the token's - to everything.

Our multi-tenant reporting query was 'optimized' last sprint. A tenant admin exported a CSV and found rows from another company in it. Here is the toy version of the table and query - what did the optimization remove?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER, tenant TEXT, total_cents INTEGER)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: OK (-1 row(s) affected)

arguments.sql: INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,'acme',12000),(2,'acme',8000),(3,'globex',99000),(4,'globex',45000)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: OK (4 row(s) affected)

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE tenant = 'acme'
SELECT SUM(total_cents) FROM orders WHERE tenant = 'acme'

messages.content:
It removed the tenant predicate. The unscoped query ranges over all 4 rows in the table; scoped to the caller's tenant it returns 2 rows summing to 20000 cents. Tenant scoping is not a filter among others; it is the isolation boundary, and it belongs in a layer that cannot be forgotten per-query: row-level security in the database, a tenant-aware ORM scope applied by default, or a data-access wrapper that refuses unscoped queries on tenant tables. Then test isolation explicitly: a fixture with two tenants and an assertion that no query path crosses over. Multi-tenant leaks are uniquely corrosive - the victim is a customer, the evidence is in their hands, and 'a refactor removed a WHERE clause' is the whole confession.

Our user-profile API returns the full user row serialized. A frontend dev noticed the JSON includes password_hash and reset_token fields. The fields are 'not displayed anywhere'. Is this a vulnerability or just untidy?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_fields=email,id,name,password_hash,reset_token
fixed_fields=email,id,name

A vulnerability, full stop. 'Not displayed' is a property of today's frontend; the API response is the product, and it is read by every client version, browser extension, proxy log, and curious user with dev tools. The buggy serializer ships buggy_fields=email,id,name,password_hash,reset_token - including a live reset_token, which is not a leak but a working account-takeover credential for anyone who can call their own profile endpoint... and then anyone else's, if an IDOR is ever found beside it.

Serialize by allowlist: name the fields a response may contain (fixed_fields=email,id,name) and build the payload from that list, never by copying the row and deleting the scary keys - denylists forget the next sensitive column the schema grows. Audit every serializer with the same question: if this JSON were posted publicly, what breaks? For anything touching credentials, the answer must be 'nothing'.

A user discovered they could make themselves admin by adding "is_admin": true to the JSON body of the update-profile request, and the ORM dutifully saved it. Which pattern is this, and what is the structural fix?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_is_admin=True
fixed_is_admin=False
fixed_name=Sammy

Mass assignment (also called auto-binding): the update copied the request body wholesale onto the model, so any column the client names becomes writable - buggy_is_admin=True. The endpoint's real contract was 'change your name and email'; the implementation's contract was 'change anything'.

The structural fix is the same allowlist discipline as serialization, on the way in: enumerate the fields this endpoint may modify and copy only those - fixed_is_admin=False while the legitimate change lands (fixed_name=Sammy). Sensitive columns (roles, balances, verification flags, owner ids) should additionally be marked non-bindable at the model layer so a future endpoint cannot expose them by accident. In review, any `update(request.body)`-shaped call is a finding on sight; in testing, every update endpoint deserves one hostile case that submits its model's most sensitive field and asserts it did not move.

Our support tool lets agents view any account (that's their job), and the same 'staff' check guards the billing-export button because 'only staff see the tool'. An agent exported the entire billing history out of curiosity. What check was too coarse?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
view_account=True
buggy_export=True
fixed_export=False

The check confused a population with a permission. 'Staff' answers 'does this person work here', but exporting billing data is a specific capability that should belong to a specific role. Because the export reused the coarse gate, buggy_export=True for every support agent - hundreds of people holding a capability the business imagined belonged to a handful.

Authorize per capability, not per container: export_fixed requires the billing role - fixed_export=False - while ordinary support work continues (view_account=True). The pattern to hunt: any `if is_staff` / `if is_employee` / `if logged_in` guarding a consequential action. Each such check is a place where convenience quietly widened a permission. And log the exports that DO happen: when a capability is bulk extraction, an audit trail of who used it is part of the control, not an extra.

Shared document links: opening a link grants viewing, which is what we want - but the same link lets the holder rename and delete the document. The link token carries no scope. How should capability links be built?

messages.content:
buggy_delete=did delete
fixed_delete=forbidden: link is view-only
fixed_view=did view

Scope the capability at mint time: the link record carries its kind (view / comment / edit), and every action checks the action against the link's scope - fixed_delete=forbidden: link is view-only, fixed_view=did view. Add the usual companions: expiry, revocation by the owner, and a list in the document's sharing panel showing which links exist with which powers. The design question to ask of any bearer artifact - link, token, key - is 'what EXACTLY does possession authorize?' If the answer is 'everything', the artifact is mis-built no matter how random its string is.

A user reset her password, then clicked the same email link again a day later 'to see what happens' - and reset it again. The token record has a used flag that the reset handler never checks. Show the flaw and the fix.

Consume the token atomically at use: check unused, mark used, change the password - one indivisible step, because a check-then-mark gap lets two simultaneous requests both pass. fixed_first=password changed to pw-one, fixed_second=invalid token. After a password reset, our user stayed signed in on a device they'd lost - the reset changed the password but their old sessions kept working, which defeats the most common reason people reset. What step did the reset flow skip?

password changed
lost_laptop_after_buggy=vic
password changed, 2 sessions killed
lost_laptop_after_fixed=None
other_user_untouched=wes

It skipped the kill. A password reset is usually a response to 'someone else may be in my account' - but a session is not the password, and changing one does not touch the other. reset_buggy changed the credential and left the lost device authenticated: the value survives as vic's session (the buggy line prints the password message while s-lost-laptop stays live).

A password change - reset or voluntary - must invalidate the account's other authenticators: sessions, remember-me tokens, refresh families (the version-stamp pattern from the remember-me case). reset_fixed reports 'password changed, 2 sessions killed', lost_laptop_after_fixed comes back empty, and other_user_untouched confirms the blast was scoped to the one account. fixed_unknown=202

Completely. The sentence is a promise the transport breaks: buggy_unknown=404 versus buggy_known=200 gives scripts the same enumeration oracle as the login form - the careful copy only protects against humans reading the page, and humans were never the enumeration threat.

Every externally visible property of the response must be identical whether or not the account exists: status (fixed_unknown=202, fixed_known=202), body, and roughly timing (queue the email asynchronously so 'known' does not return slower). If the mobile app needs to guide its user, the honest guidance is the same sentence the form shows - mobile users mistype emails too, and 'check your inbox and your spelling' serves them without informing anyone else. Internally, of course, log the truth; externally, one flat response.

Our reset email builds its link as https://{host}/reset?token=... where {host} comes straight from the request's Host header. A reviewer calls this 'host-header poisoning'. Explain, at the mechanism level, what an attacker gains and what the fix is.

CANONICAL = "app.example.com"
def link_buggy(host, tok):
    return "https://" + host + "/reset?token=" + tok
def link_fixed(host, tok):
    return "https://" + CANONICAL + "/reset?token=" + tok
print("normal=" + link_buggy("app.example.com", "rst-5"))
print("poisoned=" + link_buggy("evil-mirror.example", "rst-5"))
print("fixed_poisoned_attempt=" + link_fixed("evil-mirror.example", "rst-5"))

poisoned=https://evil-mirror.example/reset?token=rst-5
fixed_poisoned_attempt=https://app.example.com/reset?token=rst-5

The mechanism: password-reset requests can be triggered for a victim's account by anyone, and if the emailed link is built from the Host header of THAT triggering request, an attacker who requests a reset for the victim - with a forged Host pointing at a lookalike domain the attacker controls - causes your system to email the victim a genuine reset token wrapped in the attacker's URL: poisoned shows the link as https://evil-mirror.example/reset?token=rst-5. A victim who clicks lands on the mirror, which harvests the token from the URL and uses it on the real site within its validity window.

The fix is to never let request data name your own service: build absolute links from configured canonical configuration - fixed_poisoned_attempt still produces the app.example.com link no matter what the request claimed. Validate Host against an allowlist at the edge as a second layer. Any place that renders your own absolute URL - emails, redirects, webhooks - gets the same rule: configuration is the only source of your name.

Our reset uses a 6-digit code, which is fine, but the verify endpoint lets you try codes as fast as you can send them, forever. A reviewer says the code's size is not the problem. Do the arithmetic and show the control that matters.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
