coverage_1000_attempts=0.001
after_11_wrong=locked - request a new code
coverage_with_10_attempts=1e-05

The reviewer is right: six digits is a million possibilities (space=1000000), and a million is plenty IF attempts are scarce - and nothing if they are free. Unlimited online guessing turns coverage into a matter of bandwidth: coverage_1000_attempts=0.001 of the space per thousand tries, and scripts do not get tired.

The control that matters is the attempt budget: count failures against the code (and account), and burn the code after a small allowance - here 10 - forcing a fresh request: after_11_wrong=locked - request a new code, and coverage_with_10_attempts=1e-05 per code issued. Pair it with a short code lifetime and throttles on code REQUESTS, so an attacker cannot simply mint fresh codes to reset the budget - the request side is where the fatigue and spam abuses live. Code length debates are a distraction until attempts are rationed; ration first, then argue about digits.

Sequence question: a user requests a reset, then remembers the password and changes it from inside the account. The earlier reset link still works afterward and sets yet another password. Why should it not?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_reset_after_change=reset done
fixed_reset_after_change=invalid - credential changed since issue
current_pw=attacker-choice

Because the token was issued against a credential state that no longer exists. The reset link attests 'the holder of this email asked to replace password-version-1'. Once the password changes by any path, that attestation is stale - and stale reset links are exactly the artifacts that accumulate in old inboxes, which is why buggy_reset_after_change=reset done is dangerous: the final password ends up attacker-choice in the demonstration's worst case.

Bind the token to the credential version at issue and reject on divergence - fixed_reset_after_change=invalid - credential changed since issue, current_pw=attacker-choice (the legitimate in-app change stands). The version stamp is the same mechanism that kills remember-me tokens on password change; one counter, many stale-artifact problems solved. Newer requests superseding older tokens is the sibling rule: at most one live reset token per account, because two live links double the excavated-email risk for zero user benefit.

Users keep reporting 'my reset link says already used before I even clicked it'. Our email security scanner pre-fetches links to scan them, and our reset page consumes the token on GET. Explain the collision and the standard page design that avoids it.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
scanner_get=password form (token consumed)
user_click_after_scanner=invalid - already used
fixed_scanner_get=confirmation page - token checked, not consumed
fixed_user_post=password changed

The collision is between two single-use assumptions: your design consumes on first GET, and the modern mail pipeline guarantees the first GET is often a machine - scanners, link unfurlers, and preview bots fetch URLs to keep users safe. scanner_get consumed the token; user_click_after_scanner=invalid - already used through no fault of the user.

The standard design separates presentation from consumption: GET validates and renders a confirmation page with a button (fixed_scanner_get), and only the human's POST - a state-changing action no scanner performs on a random form - consumes the token and sets the password: fixed_user_post=password changed. The general law: GETs must be safe and idempotent, and any flow that punishes prefetching (one-click unsubscribe faced the same issue) will break in a world of security scanners. Design for the pipeline your email actually travels through, not the one from 2005.

Our resets table stores the reset token itself, in plaintext, next to the user id. Passwords we hash carefully. A dev argues tokens are 'not passwords' so plaintext is fine. Settle it with the toy table.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE resets (user TEXT, token TEXT)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: OK (-1 row(s) affected)

arguments.sql: INSERT INTO resets VALUES ('amy','rst-live-101'),('ben','rst-live-102')

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: OK (2 row(s) affected)

arguments.sql: SELECT token FROM resets WHERE user = 'amy'

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: rst-live-101

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM resets

messages.content:
The dev's distinction does not survive contact with the table: the query returns rst-live-101, a string that - presented to the reset endpoint - changes Amy's password. Anything that authenticates is a credential, whatever its field name, and a read-only database leak (backup, replica, SQL injection with SELECT only) converts directly into account takeover for all 2 sampled accounts without cracking anything.

Store reset tokens the way you store passwords, adjusted for their nature: tokens are high-entropy and machine-generated, so a fast cryptographic hash (SHA-256) suffices - no slow KDF needed, since there is no dictionary to grind - and look the token up by its hash. The plaintext exists in exactly one place: the email. Sessions ids and API keys deserve the same question in audit: 'if this table leaks, what can the reader DO?' For every bearer artifact, the answer should be 'nothing without also cracking hashes'.

Our reset flow lets a signed-in user change their account email with no verification, and a password reset then goes to the new address. An auditor chained these into an account-takeover path. Walk the chain and name the break point.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
reset_destination=reset link sent to attacker@example.com
fixed_change=verification link sent to attacker@example.com; address unchanged until verified
email_after_fixed_attempt=owner@example.com

The chain: any transient access to the signed-in account (borrowed laptop, stolen session) changes the email to the attacker's address with no proof the address is theirs - then the reset flow, doing its job correctly, delivers a password reset to reset_destination=reset link sent to attacker@example.com, converting minutes of session access into permanent account ownership. Each step looked acceptable alone; the composition is the vulnerability.

The break point is the email change: a new address must be verified (link clicked from the new inbox) before it becomes the account's address of record, and security mail - reset links, change notices - keeps going to the OLD verified address until then: fixed_change leaves email_after_fixed_attempt=owner@example.com. Add the companions: notify the old address of the change, and treat email change as a sensitive action requiring fresh authentication. Auditors chain small acceptances; defenders have to review compositions, not just components.

Our TOTP check accepts codes from a wide window 'to be forgiving about clock drift'. The toy implementation below derives codes per 30-second step with HMAC - count how many distinct codes are valid at once under our window versus a tight one, and judge us.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
window_plusminus_10_count=21
window_plusminus_1_count=3
guessing_surface_ratio=7.0

Judgment: the window is doing the attacker's work. A +/-10-step window means 21 consecutive 30-second codes are simultaneously valid - window_plusminus_10_count=21 distinct codes in the toy count - against +/-1 step's 3: a guessing_surface_ratio of about 7.0x, and each accepted code also stays valid for ten minutes of wall-clock time. Forgiveness for drift has quietly multiplied the value of every brute-force attempt and every phished code.

Real clocks drift by seconds, not minutes: +/-1 step (the common standard) absorbs honest drift, especially paired with a per-user drift correction learned from successful logins. This demo's HMAC construction is a toy at demo parameters - production TOTP follows RFC 6238 with a proper secret store - but the window arithmetic is identical in the real thing: every step of window is a multiplier on the guessing surface, and it should be bought only with evidence of actual drift.

Our backup recovery codes are checked against a list, but using one doesn't remove it. A user 'tested' the same code four times over a month and it worked every time. What's the correct lifecycle of a backup code?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_uses=4
fixed_first=True
fixed_second=False
codes_remaining=2

A backup code is a single-use password by another name, and its lifecycle is: generated in a batch, stored hashed, accepted exactly once, then destroyed. The buggy check treats the list as a password file that never changes - buggy_uses=4 successful uses of one code - so a photographed or shoulder-surfed code is a permanent back door that bypasses the second factor it was meant to restore.

Consume on use: fixed_first=True, fixed_second=False, and the pool visibly shrinks (codes_remaining=2), which powers the honest UX around it - showing the user how many codes remain, warning when the pool runs low, and regenerating a fresh batch (invalidating the old) on demand. Also notify the account holder whenever a backup code is used: legitimate use is rare and memorable, so the alert costs nothing and catches the other kind.

A user reported approving none of the 14 push approvals that arrived at 2am, then - exhausted - tapped approve on the 15th 'to make it stop', and an attacker was in. Our push log is the evidence. What pattern should the system itself have caught, and what design blunts it?

arguments.code:
pushes = [{"n": i, "approved": False} for i in range(1, 15)]
pushes.append({"n": 15, "approved": True})
denied = sum(1 for p in pushes if not p["approved"])
print("denied_before_approval=" + str(denied))
print("total_pushes=" + str(len(pushes)))
def policy(events):
    d = sum(1 for e in events if not e["approved"])
    return "halt pushes and require another factor" if d >= 3 else "continue"
print("policy_after_3_denials=" + policy(pushes[:3]))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
denied_before_approval=14
total_pushes=15
policy_after_3_denials=halt pushes and require another factor

The pattern is MFA fatigue (push bombing): denied_before_approval=14 refusals followed by one approval, out of total_pushes=15 in a burst. A human denying fourteen times is not 'almost authenticated' - they are under attack, and the fifteenth tap is surrender, not consent. A system that keeps pushing after repeated denials is collaborating.

Two blunts, best together. Rate-limit and react: after a few denials (policy_after_3_denials=halt pushes and require another factor), stop pushing, notify through another channel, and require a different factor - an attacker who cannot trigger pushes cannot wear the user down. And number matching: the approval screen asks the user to type or pick the number shown on the LOGIN screen, which a blind tap cannot satisfy and which ties the approval to a login the user actually started. Push approval without context is a doorbell anyone can ring until someone answers.

Audit finding: our login requires password + TOTP, but 'account recovery' requires only the answers to two security questions - mother's maiden name and first pet. The auditor says recovery is 'the real login'. Do you agree?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
login_strength=4
recovery_strength=0
weakest_path_governs=0

The auditor is right, and the toy scoring shows why: login_strength=4 on this rough scale, recovery_strength=0 - and an attacker shops at the cheapest door, so weakest_path_governs=0. Security questions are not a factor at all in any modern sense: the answers are low-entropy, often publicly discoverable (social media, data breaches, genealogy sites), unchangeable when compromised, and shared across sites.

The principle: every path that ends in an authenticated session or a credential reset must be at least as strong as the path it bypasses. Modern recovery uses possession proofs (a link or code to the verified email/phone on file), waiting periods with notifications for sensitive accounts, or identity proofing proportional to the account's value. Retire knowledge questions entirely; where regulators or legacy constraints keep them, treat them as an identifier check that triggers the real recovery flow, never as the flow itself.

Our SMS login codes have no attempt limit - same six digits, try forever, code lives 10 minutes. Sound familiar? It's the reset-code problem again, but quantify the MFA version: how much of the space can one determined script cover in the code's lifetime at 5 tries a second?

arguments.code:
SPACE = 10**6
RATE, LIFETIME = 5, 600
attempts_possible = RATE * LIFETIME
print("attempts_in_lifetime=" + str(attempts_possible))
print("coverage=" + str(attempts_possible / SPACE))
LIMIT = 5
print("coverage_with_limit_5=" + str(LIMIT / SPACE))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
attempts_in_lifetime=3000
coverage=0.003
coverage_with_limit_5=5e-06

In ten minutes at five tries a second a script makes attempts_in_lifetime=3000 guesses - coverage=0.003 of the million-code space. A 0.3% chance per code sounds small until the attacker requests codes repeatedly, targets many accounts at once, and plays a lottery that runs all day; across a thousand targeted accounts, several fall. 'Six digits' was never the control - the attempt budget is.

Cap verification attempts per code (coverage_with_limit_5=5e-06 at a limit of five) and burn the code at the cap; throttle code requests per account and per number; alert on request bursts. And design the failure honestly: legitimate users mistype, transcribe slowly, and lose signal - so a burned code should be one tap to replace, with the replacement invalidating the old. Friction belongs on the attacker's loop (unbounded, automated), not on the human's (bounded, occasional).

Our TOTP enrollment stores each user's secret in the users table in plaintext, and - an intern discovered - the seed generator handed the SAME secret to a batch of users who enrolled during one deploy. Name both defects and their distinct consequences.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
distinct_secrets=1
u1_code=869250
u2_code=869250
codes_match=True

Two distinct defects. First, shared secrets: distinct_secrets=1 across three users, so their authenticators are interchangeable - codes_match=True - meaning one user's TOTP proves every batched user's identity, and a leak of any one seed compromises the batch. A TOTP secret must be generated per user, from a CSPRNG, at enrollment; identical seeds are the fingerprint of a broken generator (a constant, a seed derived from something guessable like the timestamp or user id, or a deploy-time fallback).

Second, plaintext storage: a TOTP secret is a permanent credential - unlike a password it cannot be hashed, because the server must compute with it. So it belongs encrypted at rest (envelope encryption with keys outside the database) or in a dedicated secrets store, with access audited. A database read leak that yields passwords-as-hashes is a bad week; one that yields live TOTP seeds silently retires your second factor for every user at once.

Our 'remember this device for 30 days' MFA cookie actually lasts forever: the cookie has an expiry, but the server-side record it points to has none, and the cookie is re-issued on every visit. Users who sold a laptop found the buyer's browser still MFA-exempt a year later. Where is the lifetime bug?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
day_365_buggy_exempt=True
day_365_fixed_exempt=False
day_10_fixed_exempt=True

The lifetime lives in the wrong layer - twice over. The cookie's 30-day expiry is client-side decoration the browser may honor or the user may never trigger; the server record, the thing actually consulted, has server_expires=None, so day_365_buggy_exempt=True. Worse, re-issuing the cookie on every visit slides the client expiry forward indefinitely, so even the decoration never fires for an active device.

Device remembrance is a credential and must carry its expiry server-side, checked on every use: exempt_fixed grants day 10 (True) and refuses day 365 (False). Decide whether the 30 days slide with activity or are absolute from enrollment - and write it down, because 'remembered forever, sliding' is how a convenience feature becomes an un-auditable permanent MFA bypass attached to hardware the user no longer owns. The devices list in account settings should show these exemptions with ages and a revoke button, same as sessions.

Our backup codes are generated as an incrementing counter run through a 'scrambling' function, starting from a value derived from the user id. A researcher who got ONE of their own codes predicted their next one. What property did the generator lack?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
code1=598000
code2=605919
predicted_next=605919
prediction_correct=True

Unpredictability. The codes are a deterministic sequence - a fixed scramble of a counter - so the mapping from one code to the next is public arithmetic: given code1=598000, an attacker inverts the scramble over a small search space and computes predicted_next=605919, which is exactly code2 (prediction_correct=True). A recovery code you can derive is not a credential; it is a puzzle.

Backup codes must be drawn from a CSPRNG, independently, with enough entropy to make guessing the control problem (and then still single-use and attempt-limited, per the neighboring records). No counters, no derivation from user ids or timestamps, no 'scrambling' - obscurity of the transform is not entropy, and any transform an attacker can run forward, they can also run backward. The same rule governs every generated secret in this batch: reset tokens, session ids, API keys. If it authenticates, it is random, or it is broken.

After account recovery completes, our flow sets a new password and quietly re-enables the account - but the attacker's existing sessions (if the recovery was itself the attack) stay alive, and the owner gets no notification anywhere. What two companions must recovery always travel with?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
password reset complete
intruder_session_after_buggy=intruder
password reset complete
sessions_after_fixed=0
notices_sent=1

Invalidation and notification - the same pair as password reset, because recovery IS a password reset with extra steps. recover_buggy changed the credential and left every session standing: intruder_session_after_buggy=intruder. If the recovery was the owner's rescue, the intruder keeps the access the rescue was meant to end; if the recovery was the attack, the owner never learns it happened.

recover_fixed travels with both companions: sessions_after_fixed=0 (every authenticator dies; the recovering device re-authenticates fresh) and notices_sent=1 - an out-of-band message to the previously verified contact points saying what changed, when, and what to do if it was not you. Notification is a security control, not customer service: it converts silent compromise into a user-reported incident while reversal is still possible. Apply the pair to email changes, MFA resets, and new-device enrollments too - every event an attacker would want to be quiet.

Support can reset a user's MFA 'after verifying identity' - the verification is the same two security questions the auditor already shredded, and the reset takes effect instantly with no notice. Compose the finding the way you'd write it for the audit report.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
gaps_found=4
gap: proofing weaker than the factor it removes
gap: no notification
gap: instant effect, no window to intervene
gap: existing sessions survive

The finding writes itself once the policy is laid out as data: gaps_found=4. In audit language: 'The MFA reset procedure permits removal of the second factor on the strength of knowledge-based answers alone - a proof weaker than the factor being removed - with instant effect, no notification to the account holder, and no termination of existing sessions. An attacker with the (publicly researchable) answers and a phished or absent password path can strip MFA silently and persistently.'

Remediation in the same register: require proofing at least as strong as the factor removed (possession of the verified contact channel, or documented identity proofing for high-value accounts), notify the holder out-of-band BEFORE or as the reset takes effect, impose a delay or step-up window for sensitive accounts during which the reset can be cancelled, and terminate sessions at reset. Support tooling is part of the authentication system - audit it with the same rigor as the login page, because attackers read the help center too.
Here's our session cookie header, verbatim from the toy app: `Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; Path=/`. An auditor tied three missing attributes to three specific attacks. Do the mapping.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
secure=False
httponly=False
samesite=False
missing_count=3

All three are missing - missing_count=3 - and each maps to a distinct attack. No Secure (secure=False): the browser will send the cookie over plain HTTP, so any network position - cafe Wi-Fi, a downgrade redirect - can harvest the session id in transit. No HttpOnly (httponly=False): any script running in the page, including an injected one from an XSS flaw, can read the id from document.cookie and exfiltrate it; the cookie outlives the XSS by the session's whole lifetime. No SameSite (samesite=False): the browser attaches the cookie to cross-site requests, which is the raw material of CSRF.

The session-cookie baseline is one line: `Set-Cookie: sid=...; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax` (Strict where flows allow). None of these flags costs functionality for a normal app; their absence is never a design choice, only an inheritance from a tutorial. Audit every cookie the app sets with the same three questions.

Our session cookie is set with Domain=.example.com 'so it works on all our subdomains'. We also host a user-content blog at blog.example.com and a legacy wiki at wiki.example.com. What did the dot buy an attacker who compromises the wiki?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
sent_to_app=True
sent_to_wiki=True
host_only_sent_to_wiki=False

It bought them your session. A Domain=.example.com cookie is attached to requests to every subdomain - sent_to_wiki=True - and, more sharply, any script or page on ANY subdomain can read and SET cookies for the parent domain. Compromise the forgotten wiki and the attacker reads session cookies as users' browsers pass through, or plants a fixed session id under the parent domain that the main app will honor (fixation with a bigger lever).

Scope cookies as narrowly as the app allows: host-only (no Domain attribute) for the main app's session - host_only_sent_to_wiki=False - and separate, differently-named cookies for any subdomain that genuinely needs shared state. The underlying principle: your cookie scope defines a trust federation among subdomains, and the weakest subdomain in it - the legacy wiki, the user-content blog - sets the security of the crown jewels. Inventory your subdomains before you federate them.
Our API reflects any Origin back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, 'to make partner integrations easy'. A partner is not who I'm worried about. Who is?

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
Anyone with a web page. Reflecting arbitrary origins WITH credentials tells every browser: 'whatever site the user is visiting may read this API's responses using the user's cookies'. A malicious page the user opens in another tab can call your API, ride the ambient session, and - crucially, unlike classic CSRF - READ the responses: account data, tokens in JSON, everything the API would tell the user. buggy_evil_origin=https://evil.example shows the header cheerfully blessing the attacker's origin.

The wildcard-plus-credentials combination is so dangerous that browsers forbid the literal `*` with credentials - reflection is the workaround that re-creates it. The fix is an allowlist of exact origins: fixed_evil={} (no headers, no access), fixed_partner=https://partner.example.com (the one real partner works). Treat additions to that list as security changes requiring review, because each listed origin becomes a place whose XSS is your data breach.
Our session cookie lacks the Secure flag, and marketing insists the site 'mostly redirects HTTP to HTTPS anyway'. Show, in a toy request flow, the request where the cookie still leaks.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
http_request_sends=True
https_request_sends=True
secure_http_sends=False

The leak is the FIRST request. Before any redirect can happen, the browser must make the plain-HTTP request - and with secure missing, it attaches the cookie to that request: http_request_sends=True. The redirect to HTTPS protects the response and everything after; the session id already crossed the network in cleartext, readable by any on-path observer, and a stolen id needs no second chance.

'Mostly redirects' misunderstands the order of events: redirects are server behavior, cookie attachment is browser behavior that happens first. The Secure flag makes the browser itself refuse the cleartext trip: secure_http_sends=False. Pair it with HSTS so browsers stop attempting HTTP at all. The general lesson repeats across this batch: transport protections must live in the artifact (cookie flags, token binding), not in the hope that surrounding infrastructure steers every request safely.

To support an embedded widget, we set the session cookie to SameSite=None. A security review now says our state-changing POST endpoints are CSRF-exposed in a way they weren't with Lax. Connect the dots.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
lax_cross_site_post=False
none_cross_site_post=True
none_requires_secure=True

SameSite is a CSRF control, and None switches it off. With Lax, the browser withholds the cookie from cross-site POSTs - lax_cross_site_post=False - which quietly neutralized classic CSRF for your POST endpoints even without tokens. Setting None for the widget's sake restores attachment everywhere: none_cross_site_post=True, so a cross-site form post or fetch now arrives fully authenticated, and any endpoint that trusts the cookie alone will act on it.

The repair is not necessarily retreating from None - embedded contexts legitimately need it (and None requires Secure, as noted) - it is replacing the lost control deliberately: anti-CSRF tokens on state-changing endpoints, or Origin/Referer checks for the API. The lesson generalizes: cookie attributes are a security posture, and changing one for a product feature silently re-prices attacks elsewhere. Any change to SameSite, Domain, or Path deserves the question 'which attack did this attribute hold back, and what holds it now?'

Login loop mystery: the browser receives our session cookie but never sends it back. The cookie is named __Host-sid but set with Path=/app and no Secure flag. The server logs show nothing wrong. Why is the browser silently discarding it?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
our_cookie_ok=False
fixed_cookie_ok=True

The browser is enforcing the __Host- prefix contract, and your cookie breaks two of its three terms. The prefix is a promise: a cookie named __Host-* must be set with Secure, Path=/, and no Domain attribute - browsers accept it only then, precisely so that a compliant cookie is guaranteed to have come from the host itself over HTTPS. Yours lacks Secure and uses Path=/app: our_cookie_ok=False, and the browser drops it without telling your server anything - hence the empty logs and the loop.

Either honor the contract (fixed_cookie_ok=True: Secure, Path=/, host-only) or drop the prefix and use a plain name with ordinary attributes. The diagnostic habit matters more than the specific rule: when a browser silently refuses state, suspect the client's enforcement rules - prefixes, SameSite=None without Secure, oversized cookies - before suspecting the server. The browser is a security actor with its own policy layer, and its rejections are silent by design.

Logout doesn't log you out in our app - but only in the admin area. The login sets the session cookie with Path=/, while the admin logout clears a cookie with Path=/admin. The cookie jar below shows why. Explain.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
jar_after_admin_logout={('sid', '/'): 'tok-live'}
jar_after_matching_clear={}

Cookies are keyed by (name, domain, path) - three parts, not one. Login created the entry ('sid', '/'), but the admin logout cleared ('sid', '/admin'), a different key that may not even exist: jar_after_admin_logout={('sid', '/'): 'tok-live'} - the real cookie sits untouched, and the browser keeps sending it. The logout 'worked' in testing from the main area (where the clearing path matched) and fails only under /admin, which is why the report sounded flaky.

Clear with the identical attributes used at set time - same name, path, and domain - as the second clear shows: jar_after_matching_clear={}. Expire it properly too (Expires in the past / Max-Age=0), because deleting by setting an empty value with a live expiry leaves a zombie empty cookie. And remember the server-side half from the logout record earlier: even a perfectly cleared cookie only completes logout when the server record dies with it. Client tidiness plus server invalidation - both, every time.

Our cookie banner release accidentally set TWO session cookies - sid on Path=/ and sid on Path=/app - during a migration, and now some requests authenticate as a stale user. The server reads 'the' sid cookie. What does the browser actually send, and what's the cleanup?

arguments.code:
sent = [("sid", "/", "tok-old"), ("sid", "/app", "tok-new")]
def server_reads(cookies):
    return cookies[0][2]
print("cookies_sent_count=" + str(len(sent)))
print("server_sees=" + server_reads(sent))
print("stale_value=" + sent[0][2])

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
cookies_sent_count=2
server_sees=tok-old
stale_value=tok-old

The browser sends both - cookies_sent_count=2 - because name alone does not identify a cookie; (name, path) pairs do, and both paths match a request under /app. The Cookie header becomes 'sid=tok-old; sid=tok-new', and most server frameworks hand you the first, the last, or a parse-order accident: server_sees=tok-old, the stale token, which is why users flip between identities depending on which path they entered through.

Cleanup has to be explicit: expire the wrong-path cookie with a Set-Cookie that names its exact path (you cannot delete it from the other path), and standardize on ONE canonical path for the session cookie - '/' unless you have a reason - enforced in a single cookie-issuing helper so no release can mint a variant. The deeper rule: every cookie attribute is part of the cookie's identity, and code that treats name as identity will eventually meet a jar that disagrees.

Our session cookie expires in 30 days, but the server-side session record expires in 24 hours. Users complain the app 'forgets' them daily despite 'remember me' marketing copy, and support blames the users' browsers. Who's right?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
promised_days=30
effective_days=1.0
aligned_effective_days=30

The users are right. A session survives only as long as BOTH halves live, so the effective lifetime is the minimum: effective_days=1.0 against promised_days=30. The browser faithfully presents a 30-day cookie every morning; the server looks up a record it deleted at hour 24 and says 'unknown session' - a daily logout wearing a remember-me costume.

Align the two lifetimes in one configuration value consumed by both the cookie issuer and the session store (aligned_effective_days=30), and if you want sliding renewal, slide both together when activity extends the session. Mismatched halves produce a special kind of support hell because every individual component is 'working': the cookie is present, the store is consistent, the code is correct - only the composition lies. When a symptom is a lifetime, print both halves' clocks first.

A pen-test note says our session id is readable from JavaScript - they ran document.cookie in the console and got it - even though 'the app is all server-rendered'. The Set-Cookie line has Secure and SameSite but not HttpOnly. Why did server-rendering not save us?

arguments.code:
header = "sid=tok-9; Path=/; Secure; SameSite=Lax"
def js_can_read(h):
    return "HttpOnly" not in h
print("js_readable=" + str(js_can_read(header)))
print("with_httponly=" + str(js_can_read(header + "; HttpOnly")))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
js_readable=True

The per-cookie size limit. Browsers guarantee roughly 4096 bytes per cookie; this one totals cookie_bytes=4440 - over_by=344 - and the browser's response is silent refusal: dropped_silently=True, no error anywhere, the login simply never sticks. The subset affected is exactly the users with the largest profiles - longest role lists, richest preferences - which is why the bug looked like an account problem and survived triage.

The architectural correction matters more than the diet: a session cookie should carry an opaque id and nothing else; profile, roles, and preferences live server-side where size is cheap and revocation works. Every byte of state moved into the cookie is state you can no longer revoke, must re-validate, and must fit through the browser's keyhole. If client-side state is genuinely needed, budget it like an engineer: measure the p99 size, keep a hard ceiling in tests, and remember the limit is per cookie and shared with every other feature team stuffing the same jar.

Redirect loop case: login succeeds at example.com, which sets the session cookie for the apex domain, and the app lives at app.example.com - which sets its OWN cookie during its boot sequence, for the host only, with the same name. Users bounce between login and app forever. Untangle it.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
distinct_cookies=2
app_sees=tok-app-boot
login_sees=tok-from-login

Two cookies, one name, and each side of the conversation reads a different one. (name, domain) makes them distinct entries - distinct_cookies=2. The app boot wrote a host-only cookie that shadows the login cookie for app.example.com requests: app_sees=tok-app-boot, an anonymous boot token, so the app concludes 'not logged in' and redirects to login; login checks its own cookie - login_sees=tok-from-login, perfectly valid - concludes 'already logged in' and redirects back. The loop is two correct local decisions about two different cookies.

Untangle by giving the session cookie exactly one home: one issuer, one domain scope (host-only on the app, or the parent domain if SSO across subdomains is the design - chosen once), and forbid other components from setting the same name. The app boot sequence has no business minting a session cookie at all; if it needs a boot token, it gets its own name. Same-name-different-scope is the cookie jar's version of the two-sid problem from the migration record: identity by name alone is the root error in both.

A user changed their account email, and our password-reset mail kept going to the OLD address for a day, which support called a bug. The change flow has a pending state. Explain why the 'bug' is the correct behavior, and what would make it an actual bug.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
reset_goes_to=old@example.com
after_confirm_reset_goes_to=new@example.com

The 'bug' is the security design working. Until the new address is verified, the address of record is still the old one - reset_goes_to=old@example.com - because the account must always have a proven channel for its most sensitive mail. If resets followed an UNVERIFIED pending address instantly, the email-change takeover chain from the reset family (hijack session, change email, reset password, own account) would be wide open.

It becomes an actual bug if any of these fail: the verification link never arrives or cannot complete (check the pending flow end-to-end), the pending state never expires (stale pending changes should die in a day or so), or - the subtle one - the user gets NO notice at the old address that a change was requested. Notice at the old address is what converts a hijack attempt into a user-reported incident. After verification, the flip is atomic: after_confirm_reset_goes_to=new@example.com, and the old address receives a final 'your email was changed' message.

We disabled a departing employee's account at 09:00 - the flag is set, login is refused - yet their already-issued access tokens kept calling the API until they expired naturally at midnight. The per-request middleware checks the token signature and expiry only. Name the missing check.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_disabled_user_api=True
fixed_disabled_user_api=False

The account-state check. Disabling was implemented at the login door only, but a stateless token does not pass the login door - it was already inside. api_buggy asks the token two questions (genuine? unexpired?) and never asks the directory the third: is this account still enabled? buggy_disabled_user_api=True for a user disabled hours ago.

This is the standing tension of stateless tokens: instant disable requires a state lookup, which is what statelessness was avoiding. The settlements, in ascending strength: keep access-token lifetimes short so the disable lag is minutes (the common production answer); maintain a small revocation/disabled list checked per request (cheap, since it is tiny and cacheable for seconds); or look the account up per request for sensitive routes only. fixed_disabled_user_api=False with the check in place. What is not acceptable is the surprise: if your disable SLA is 'at token expiry', write THAT in the offboarding runbook so HR's 09:00 expectation matches the system's midnight reality.

Our remember-me implementation stores a single token per user in the database, in plaintext, and compares it directly. The better pattern splits the token into selector and validator. Explain, with the toy, what the split buys when the database leaks.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
db_row_contains_usable_token=False
fixed_lookup=True
fixed_wrong=False

The split separates finding from proving. The selector is a public lookup key - it names the row and is safe to expose. The validator is the secret, and the database stores only its hash: db_row_contains_usable_token=False, so a leaked table yields selectors and hashes, none of which can be presented as a working cookie. Verification hashes the presented validator and compares: fixed_lookup=True, fixed_wrong=False.

Two more dividends. Theft detection: with the validator rotating on every use under a stable selector, a replayed OLD validator proves two parties hold the token - the reuse-detection pattern from the refresh-token family, available here for free. And scoping: one user can hold many selector rows (one per device), so revocation is per-device instead of nuclear. The single-plaintext-token design gets none of this: leak equals compromise, reuse is invisible, revocation is all-or-nothing. Remember-me tokens are long-lived by design, which is exactly why they deserve the strongest storage pattern in the building.

Account merge bug: support merged a duplicate account into a primary. The duplicate's sessions were re-pointed to the primary's user id - but the duplicate's REMEMBER-ME token still resolves to the merged-away identity in one legacy table, and using it resurrects a ghost session as the wrong user. What's the general lesson?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
remember_result=ghost session as duplicate
fixed_result=rejected: identity merged away - token revoked

The lesson: identity lifecycle operations - merge, disable, delete, rename - must enumerate every authenticator that can resolve to the identity, in every table that grew one over the years. The merge updated the sessions table and missed the legacy remember-me table, leaving a live credential pointing at a dead identity: remember_result=ghost session as duplicate. A merged-away user should be a black hole: nothing resolves to it, nothing authenticates as it.

Practically: the merge (and disable, and deletion) procedure needs a checklist generated from the schema, not from memory - every table with a user foreign key gets a row in the runbook with its disposition (re-point, revoke, delete). And resolvers should fail closed on inactive identities as the second line of defense: fixed_result=rejected: identity merged away - token revoked. Ghost identities are what happen when 'user' is a row in one table in the design doc and a dozen references in the real system.

Our login rate limiter counts attempts per USERNAME across the whole platform. Two unrelated companies both have a user 'admin', and one company's attacker keeps locking the other's admin out. Also, the same person with accounts 'Lee' and 'lee' gets double budget. Dissect the keying error.

from collections import defaultdict
counts = defaultdict(int)
def hit_buggy(tenant, username):
    counts[username] += 1
    return counts[username]
for _ in range(5):
    hit_buggy("acme", "admin")
print("globex_admin_budget_used_by_acme_attacker=" + str(hit_buggy("globex", "admin") - 1))
counts.clear()
def hit_fixed(tenant, username):
    key = (tenant, username.strip().lower())
    counts[key] += 1
    return counts[key]
for _ in range(5):
    hit_fixed("acme", "admin")
print("fixed_globex_admin_count=" + str(counts[("globex", "admin")]))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
globex_admin_budget_used_by_acme_attacker=5
fixed_globex_admin_count=0

The limiter keyed on a name that is neither unique nor canonical. Usernames are unique per tenant (or per system), not per planet: keying globally lets one tenant's attacker spend another tenant's budget - globex_admin_budget_used_by_acme_attacker=5 of the second tenant's allowance consumed by a stranger. And because the key is the raw string, 'Lee' and 'lee' are two budgets for one human - the normalization lesson from the credential family, recurring in limiter form.

Key limiters on the same identity the AUTH system uses: (tenant, normalized username), plus the source dimension from the lockout record - fixed_globex_admin_count=0, an untouched budget. The meta-rule is worth stating plainly: any component that counts, caches, or keys by identity must import the identity definition from the one place that owns it. Every hand-rolled re-derivation - raw username here, IP there, unnormalized email elsewhere - eventually disagrees with the real identity at the worst moment.

Our OIDC login flow generates a state value, stores it, and sends it to the provider - but the callback handler never compares the returned state to the stored one. 'It's just a random string, the code exchange is the secure part.' Grade that claim at the mechanism level.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy_foreign_flow=session created for code holder
fixed_foreign_flow=rejected: state mismatch
fixed_own_flow=session created for code holder

The claim fails. State is the CSRF token of the login flow: it binds the callback to the browser that STARTED the flow. Without the comparison, an attacker can start a flow with their own provider account, capture the resulting callback URL (with a valid code for the ATTACKER's identity), and trick a victim's browser into visiting it - the victim's app exchanges the code and creates a session, in the victim's browser, bound to the attacker's account: buggy_foreign_flow=session created for code holder. Everything the victim then does - saved payment methods, entered data - lands in the attacker's account. Login CSRF, gift-wrapped.

With the comparison, the foreign flow dies - fixed_foreign_flow=rejected: state mismatch - because the victim's stored state cannot match the attacker's, while the genuine flow passes: fixed_own_flow=session created for code holder. Generating a security value and not verifying it is a recurring costume in this batch (the unused 'used' flag, the unchecked exp): the ceremony was performed, the check was not. In review, for every stored nonce, state, or flag, demand to see the comparison.

Usability bug with a security flavor: the app shows 'you will be signed out in 5 minutes' at minute 25, but the server session TTL is 20 minutes - users lose long forms at minute 20 with the warning still pending. Two config values again. What's the correct relationship?

warn_at = 25

print("fixed_warn_at=" + str(server_ttl2 - warn_margin))

fixed_warn_at=25

The warning is scheduled after the event it warns about: warning_ever_shown=False, because warn_at (25) exceeds the server's TTL (20) - the session is already dead before the countdown begins. Users experience this as the app lying, and they lose exactly the long, valuable work the warning existed to protect.

The correct relationship is one source of truth: the client learns the expiry from the server (a field in the session response), and the warning is DERIVED - fixed_warn_at=25, always TTL minus a margin - never an independent constant someone typed into the frontend. The same derivation discipline applies to the refresh moment and the 'session expired' message. Whenever two numbers must agree for the user experience to be honest, one of them must be computed from the other; two hand-maintained constants are a promise to drift, and drift in session UX teaches users to ignore warnings - including the ones that matter.

The finding: passwords_in_logs=3 of lines=5 sampled - every failed attempt writes the attempted password in plaintext to a system with far wider access than the credential store: log aggregation, support tooling, vendor pipelines, backups. Then treat the existing logs as a credential exposure: restrict, expire them early, and force-reset for any account whose cleartext appears - starting with the ones that look one typo away from a success. Debugging convenience is not a control; it is how controls get bypassed.

Capstone: you are auditing a small composed auth subsystem - session store, reset flow, a route handler, a cookie, and a token verifier, all modeled below. Five defects from five different families are planted. Run the audit, name all five, and pair each with its fix.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
findings=5
finding: 1. sessions never expire (200-day session still live)
finding: 2. reset token reusable after first use
finding: 3. role trusted from client request
finding: 4. session cookie missing Secure/HttpOnly
finding: 5. token expiry never checked

All five, each from a different family. 1. Session lifecycle: a 200-day session still authenticates because the store has no TTL - fix with absolute and idle expiry checked per request, plus a sweeper. 2. Reset flow: the used flag is written but never read, so the token resets repeatedly - fix by consuming atomically at use. 3. Authorization: the handler trusts a role field from the request body - fix by deriving roles from the server-side record for the authenticated identity. 4. Cookie hygiene: the session cookie lacks Secure and HttpOnly - fix with the full baseline attribute set. 5. Token validation: the verifier checks the signature and stops, accepting an expired token - fix by validating claims (exp, iss, aud, type) after the signature.

The meta-lesson of the capstone is that none of these required exotic skill to plant or to find - each is a missing line, an unread flag, an unchecked claim. Auth systems rarely fall to genius attacks on strong code; they fall to ordinary code where one expected check was never written. The audit method that finds them is equally ordinary: enumerate the artifacts (sessions, tokens, resets, cookies, roles), and for each one ask who can create it, what limits its lifetime, what limits its power, and where those limits are enforced. Five questions, five findings.
